title: Shifting Power and the Causes of World War I
subject: AP World History
objectives: Explain how internal and external factors shifted the global balance of power after 1900 (decline of land-based empires, rise of new powers)
Analyze the long-term causes of World War I using the M.A.I.N. framework (militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism)
Distinguish the underlying causes of World War I from its immediate trigger (the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand)
Describe how the alliance system and imperial rivalries turned a regional crisis into a global war

sections.heading: A Wrong Turn on a Sarajevo Street
sections.content:
On the morning of June 28, 1914, a teenage Bosnian Serb named Gavrilo Princip had already failed. He was one of several young assassins who had set out that day to kill Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of the sprawling Austro-Hungarian Empire, as the Archduke's motorcade rolled through the city of Sarajevo. A bomb had been thrown earlier and missed. The plot seemed to have collapsed, and a discouraged Princip wandered off to a sandwich shop. Then chance intervened. The Archduke's driver, confused about the route, took a wrong turn onto the very street where Princip was standing, and stopped the car to reverse. Princip stepped forward and fired twice. Within an hour, Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie were dead.

Within six weeks, the major powers of Europe were at war, and within a few years that war had pulled in soldiers and colonies from across Africa, Asia, the Pacific, and the Americas, killing roughly seventeen million people. How does a single shooting in a Balkan city become a global catastrophe? The answer is that the bullet did not cause the war so much as ignite it. Europe in 1914 was a room filled with gunpowder, and the assassination was merely the spark. This lesson is about all the gunpowder — the long-term pressures that had been building for decades and made a massive war not just possible but, many feared, almost inevitable.

This is also the opening of the final period of the course (c. 1900–present), and it begins with a shift in the global balance of power. The land-based empires that had dominated earlier units — the Ottomans, the Qing, the Russian and Austro-Hungarian empires — were weakening or collapsing, while industrialized nation-states, fired by nationalism and armed with the deadly technology of Unit 5, jostled for dominance. Understanding why World War I broke out means understanding this larger transformation: an old world order coming apart, and a new and dangerous one taking its place.

sections.heading: A Changing Balance of Power
sections.content:
By 1900, the global distribution of power looked very different from the world of 1750 you studied in earlier units. Several of the great land-based and Islamic empires were in serious decline. The OTTOMAN EMPIRE, once a superpower straddling three continents, had shrunk and weakened so badly that Europeans dismissively called it the 'sick man of Europe'; it was losing territory in the Balkans and North Africa and surviving partly because the great powers could not agree on how to divide it. QING CHINA had been humiliated by the Opium Wars, the unequal treaties, and the Boxer Rebellion (Unit 6), and would fall entirely in 1911. RUSSIA, though enormous, was an autocratic, only partly industrialized empire shaken by revolution in 1905 and by a humiliating defeat in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905.

As old powers faltered, new ones rose. GERMANY, unified only in 1871, had industrialized with astonishing speed and by 1900 had surpassed Britain in steel and chemical production. It was a young, ambitious, powerful state that wanted colonies, naval power, and recognition as a world leader — a demand that unsettled the established powers, especially Britain. The UNITED STATES had become an industrial giant and, after the Spanish-American War of 1898, an overseas imperial power. And JAPAN, having modernized through the Meiji Restoration, stunned the world by defeating Russia in 1905 — the first time in modern history that an Asian power had beaten a European great power in a full-scale war, a result that electrified anti-colonial movements across Asia and Africa.

This is the crucial backdrop to World War I: a world in which the relative power of states was shifting fast, in which rising powers demanded a bigger place and declining ones clung to what they had, and in which the most dangerous flashpoint of all was the Balkans — a region of small, newly independent, fiercely nationalist states wedged between the collapsing Ottoman Empire and the multi-ethnic Austro-Hungarian Empire. The Balkans had earned the nickname 'the powder keg of Europe,' and it was there, in Sarajevo, that the spark would fall.

sections.question: Why is the period around 1900 best described as a time of 'shifting global power'?
options: Every empire in the world was growing stronger at the same rate
Older land-based empires (Ottoman, Qing, Russian, Austro-Hungarian) were weakening or collapsing while industrialized states like Germany, the U.S., and Japan rose rapidly
Europe lost all of its colonies before 1900
The global balance of power had not changed since 1750
sections.explanation: Around 1900 the balance of power was shifting fast: the old land-based and Islamic empires (Ottoman, Qing, Russian, Austro-Hungarian) were weakening or fragmenting, while newly industrialized states — a unified Germany, the United States, and Meiji Japan — rose rapidly and demanded a larger role. Japan's 1905 defeat of Russia symbolized the shift.

sections.heading: The Long-Term Causes: M.A.I.N.
sections.content:
Historians organize the long-term causes of World War I with a famous and exam-friendly acronym: M.A.I.N. — Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, and Nationalism. None of these alone caused the war; together, over decades, they turned Europe into the powder keg.

MILITARISM was the glorification of military power and the belief that a strong, ready military was the key to national greatness. The great powers poured resources into building larger armies and navies, drew up detailed war plans, and treated war as a legitimate and even noble instrument of policy. The most dramatic example was the naval ARMS RACE between Britain and Germany, especially after Germany began building modern battleships (dreadnoughts) to challenge British naval supremacy. ALLIANCES bound the powers into two armed camps: the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy, and the Triple Entente of France, Russia, and Britain. These alliances were meant to deter war by balancing power, but they had a fatal flaw — they could turn a small, local conflict into a general one by dragging every member in. A quarrel between two states could automatically pull in four more.

IMPERIALISM (Unit 6) fueled bitter rivalry and resentment. The great powers competed fiercely for colonies, markets, and prestige, and clashes over Morocco and other territories repeatedly raised tensions and hardened the sense that the powers were enemies. Germany in particular felt it had arrived too late to the colonial scramble and resented Britain's and France's vast empires. NATIONALISM, finally, was the combustible emotional fuel. It made citizens proud, aggressive, and eager to prove their nation's superiority, and it made the great powers willing to risk war over prestige. Most dangerously, in the Balkans, nationalism took the form of demands by Slavic peoples — backed by Russia — for independence from the Austro-Hungarian Empire. It was this Balkan nationalism that loaded the gun that Gavrilo Princip fired.

sections.heading: The M.A.I.N. Causes of World War I
rows: Glorifying military power; arms buildup and war planning
Two armed camps that could pull all members into war
Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) vs. Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain)
Rivalry over colonies, markets, and prestige
Crises over Morocco; German resentment of British/French empires
Aggressive pride; demands for self-rule by ethnic groups
Slavic nationalism in the Balkans, backed by Russia, against Austria-Hungary
The spark, not an underlying cause
Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, June 28, 1914

sections.content: World War I had deep, long-term causes — Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, and Nationalism (M.A.I.N.) — that turned Europe into a 'powder keg'; the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914 was only the immediate spark that ignited it.

sections.heading: From a Spark to a World War: The July Crisis
sections.content:
Watch how the underlying causes converted one assassination into a continental war in just over a month — a chain reaction historians call the July Crisis. After Franz Ferdinand's murder, Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia (the assassins had ties to a Serbian nationalist group) and saw a chance to crush Serbian nationalism for good. Backed by a 'blank check' of unconditional support from Germany, Austria-Hungary issued Serbia an ultimatum so harsh it was designed to be rejected, and then declared war on Serbia on July 28, 1914.

Now the ALLIANCES did their fatal work. Russia, the self-appointed protector of its fellow Slavs in Serbia, began mobilizing its army. Germany, bound to Austria-Hungary and fearing encirclement between Russia and France, declared war on Russia and then on France. To attack France quickly, Germany's war plan (the Schlieffen Plan) called for invading through neutral BELGIUM — and Germany's violation of Belgian neutrality brought BRITAIN into the war against Germany. Within a week of Austria's declaration on tiny Serbia, all the great powers of Europe were at war. The alliance system, meant to keep the peace through deterrence, instead acted like a row of dominoes.

This sequence is the perfect illustration of the difference between an immediate cause and underlying causes — a distinction the AP exam tests constantly. The assassination was the immediate trigger, but it only led to world war because of the militarism, alliances, imperial rivalries, and nationalism that had been building for decades. Remove the gunpowder, and the spark fizzles out; many assassinations and crises had occurred before without causing a world war. The deeper forces are what made 1914 different.

sections.question: What is the BEST way to describe the role of the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in causing World War I?
options: It was the single underlying cause of the war
It was the immediate trigger (spark) that set off a war made possible by deeper causes like militarism, alliances, imperialism, and nationalism
It had no real connection to the outbreak of the war
It caused the war entirely on its own, with no other factors involved
sections.explanation: The assassination was the immediate trigger, not an underlying cause. It led to a world war only because of the long-term M.A.I.N. pressures (militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism) that had primed Europe for conflict. Distinguishing the spark from the underlying 'gunpowder' is a core causation skill the exam rewards.

sections.heading: Tracing the Alliance Dominoes, Day by Day
sections.content:
Let's read the July Crisis of 1914 the way a historian reconstructs a causal chain, watching one event topple the next. The trigger is June 28: Gavrilo Princip assassinates Franz Ferdinand. For nearly a month, little visibly happens — but behind the scenes Austria-Hungary secures Germany's 'blank check' of unconditional backing. On July 23, Austria-Hungary issues Serbia a deliberately impossible ultimatum; on July 28, it declares war on Serbia. So far this looks like a small Balkan quarrel.

Now watch the alliances convert it into a continental war. Russia, protector of its fellow Slavs, begins mobilizing its huge army. Germany, bound to Austria-Hungary and terrified of being caught between Russia and France, declares war on Russia (August 1) and then on France (August 3). To beat France fast, Germany executes the Schlieffen Plan and invades neutral Belgium — and that violation brings Britain in against Germany on August 4. In a single week, a murder in Sarajevo had become a war among all the great powers.

Here is the analytical payoff. Read in isolation, each step seems almost reasonable — a state honoring its commitments, defending an ally, following its war plan. But the SYSTEM was the problem: the rigid alliance structure meant that no leader could stop at one step without abandoning an ally and appearing weak. This is why historians say the assassination did not 'cause' the war so much as activate a machine already built for it. When you analyze causation, look not only at the trigger but at the SYSTEM that converted a local event into a catastrophe — that system, here the alliances and mobilization timetables, is the real underlying cause.

sections.heading: Separating Underlying Causes from Triggers (a Causation Skill)

steps.title: Identify the immediate trigger
steps.content: First name the spark — the specific event that set things in motion. For WWI, that is the assassination of Franz Ferdinand (June 1914) and the July Crisis. The trigger is necessary to explain timing ('why 1914?') but does not by itself explain the war's scale.

steps.title: List the underlying (long-term) causes
steps.content: Next, identify the deeper conditions that built up over years or decades. For WWI, use M.A.I.N.: militarism (arms race), alliances (two armed camps), imperialism (colonial rivalry), and nationalism (especially in the Balkans). These explain WHY a spark could become a catastrophe.

steps.title: Explain the relationship between them
steps.content: Show how the trigger interacted with the underlying causes: the assassination activated the alliance system, which converted a Balkan quarrel into a war among all the great powers. A strong answer connects the spark to the gunpowder rather than treating them as separate lists.

steps.title: Weigh and prioritize for a thesis
steps.content: Take a defensible position about which causes mattered most — for example, 'While the assassination triggered the war, the alliance system was the mechanism that made it global.' Prioritizing causes, rather than listing them as equal, is what earns the top causation score.

sections.heading: Don't Confuse the Trigger with the Cause
sections.content: The most common WWI mistake on the AP exam is treating the assassination of Franz Ferdinand as 'the cause' of the war. It was the immediate TRIGGER. An essay or MCQ answer that stops there misses the point: the war became a world war because of long-term militarism, alliances, imperialism, and nationalism. A second frequent error is chronology — placing the Russo-Japanese War (1904–05), the alliance system, and the naval arms race AFTER 1914 rather than before. These pressures BUILT UP over the decades BEFORE the war. Finally, do not assume WWI was a purely 'European' war: it pulled in colonies and troops from Africa, Asia, and the Pacific (covered in the next lesson), and the shifting balance of power was global.

sections.heading: Use M.A.I.N. — but Make It an Argument
sections.content: M.A.I.N. (Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism) is a reliable way to organize the long-term causes of WWI on an SAQ or LEQ, and graders recognize it. But do not just list the four words. Turn them into an argument by categorizing and weighing: explain which cause mattered most and how the causes reinforced one another (e.g., nationalism in the Balkans + the alliance system = a local crisis becoming a continental war). For an SAQ asking for a cause of WWI, give ONE specific cause with a SPECIFIC example (e.g., 'the British-German naval arms race' rather than just 'militarism').

sections.heading: Causes of WWI Essentials
sections.content: SHIFTING POWER c. 1900: declining land-based/Islamic empires (OTTOMAN = 'sick man of Europe,' QING China falls 1911, autocratic RUSSIA) vs. rising industrial powers (unified GERMANY since 1871, the U.S., and MEIJI JAPAN — which defeated Russia in 1904–05). LONG-TERM CAUSES = M.A.I.N.: MILITARISM (British-German naval/dreadnought arms race); ALLIANCES (Triple Alliance: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy vs. Triple Entente: France, Russia, Britain); IMPERIALISM (colonial rivalry, e.g., Morocco crises); NATIONALISM (esp. Slavic nationalism in the BALKANS, the 'powder keg of Europe'). IMMEDIATE TRIGGER: assassination of Archduke FRANZ FERDINAND in SARAJEVO by Gavrilo Princip, June 28, 1914 → July Crisis → alliance dominoes → world war. Key distinction: TRIGGER (assassination) vs. UNDERLYING causes (M.A.I.N.).

sections.heading: Why the Causes of WWI Still Matter
sections.content:
World War I is sometimes called 'the seminal catastrophe of the twentieth century,' and the phrase is not an exaggeration. Almost everything you will study in the rest of this course flows, directly or indirectly, from this war and the way it began. The collapse of four empires (German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, and Ottoman), the Russian Revolution and the birth of the Soviet Union, the harsh peace that helped produce Hitler, the redrawing of the Middle East's borders, and the first cracks in European colonial empires all trace back to the conflict ignited in Sarajevo. If you understand why WWI happened, you hold the key to the entire final period of the course.

The deeper lesson is about how catastrophes happen at all. The story of 1914 is a warning about systems that are rigid, over-armed, and bound by automatic commitments. The alliance system was designed to prevent war through deterrence, yet its very rigidity ensured that once one domino fell, all of them did; leaders felt trapped by mobilization timetables and obligations they had built themselves. Historians and political scientists still study July 1914 as a case study in how miscalculation, nationalism, and interlocking commitments can drag reluctant nations into a war that almost no one actually wanted in the form it took. During the Cold War (Unit 8), leaders on both sides consciously studied 1914 precisely to avoid stumbling into a nuclear version of it.

For the exam, this lesson trains the single most tested historical-reasoning skill of the unit: CAUSATION, and specifically the distinction between long-term underlying causes and immediate triggers. That distinction will return for the causes of World War II, the Cold War, and decolonization. Master it here, with the vivid example of the powder keg and the spark, and you will be ready to deploy it across the whole modern period — including in the unit's synthesis lesson, where you will use it to build a full causation argument.
